Between these factions, edicts are carried out through carefully negotiated weather events: a moral quandary delivered as drizzle, policy shifts proclaimed as microbursts. Thunder exists only as rumor—a myth of volume no one here has ever heard, yet everyone claims to recall.

I submit this report with caution. To exit, I must ride a refracted beam of sunlight through the drop’s equatorial tension. Yet every moment spent charting this impossible geography pulls me deeper into its cyclical logic. If I fail to return, know that I left a map etched in the Prism Ranges—visible only at the angle of longing.

Until retrieval,

In the middle of a fern-laced clearing somewhere around 150 million years B.C., Winifred Burke first discovered—much to her annoyance—that the Library Stabilizer had misfiled her in the Jurassic instead of pre-war Vienna. In fairness, the Stabilizer was overdue for calibration, but still, the woman had a schedule.

“I suppose the opera will have to wait,” she sighed, straightening her anachronistic tweed cardigan. The air smelled of damp moss and impending thunder, but the clear moral imperative was unmistakable: when stranded, always establish a book club. She set her brass pocket watch to local sun-noon, laid a tartan picnic blanket over an obligingly flat rock, and unpacked her traveling chest of curated literature.

Recruiting members required the sort of diplomatic finesse generally reserved for interlibrary loan negotiations. The first candidate lumbered through the cycads with a curiosity Winifred instantly recognized: a Brachiosaurus, a gentle four-story-tall herbivore whose eyes twinkled with the look of someone (technically some dinosaur) who secretly preferred poetry. She coaxed it closer with a wreath of ginkgo leaves. “Welcome,” she declared, “to the Portage Avenue Chapter of the Intertemporal Book Society.” The Brachiosaurus—she named him Bernard, to streamline minutes-taking—considered the invitation, sneezed a jet of Jurassic pollen, and seated himself in a manner as cozy as several tons of dinosaur could manage.

The second participant, an Allosaurus lurking behind a stand of horsetails, presented a different challenge—a discerning palate and far too many teeth. Winifred identified her as more of a narrative nonfiction reader. “Do you enjoy scandalous footnotes?” Winifred asked, offering a battered copy of “The Etiquette of Cretaceous Predation.” The Allosaurus emitted a bemused grumble, which Winifred took as assent. She christened her Ada.

Finally, after much coaxing, a flock of Compsognathus arrived, drawn by the promise of warmed pinecone tea and leftover scones. Winifred promised every chapter a cliffhanger and two crumbs.

When the meeting commenced, Winifred passed around a few modern paperbacks (carefully laminated against the humidity): a novel about fossil hunters, a botanical field guide, and—ambitiously—a slim volume of poetry. Her opening remarks were standard: “Good evening and welcome to all species, carbon-dated or otherwise. Please silence any guttural roars until discussion time.” Bernard obligingly bent down and flipped pages with a dexterity surprising for someone lacking fingers. Ada adjusted her tail and attempted a skeptical expression, which, given the jawline, could also have been hunger. The Compsognathus merely peeped.

The first assignment: a serial novel called “Chronicles of the Young Fern.” Bernard went first, offering a series of basso rumbles that Winifred dutifully recorded as detailed character analysis. (“Bernard appreciates the fern protagonist’s struggle with overstory shading—notes on canopy dynamics.”) When Ada recounted her impression—short bursts of guttural chirps—Winifred translated this as a critique of the pacing: “Prefers more chases, fewer polysyllabic descriptions.” She made a note: Next meeting, perhaps introduce non-fiction on marine reptiles?

After the literary discussion, Winifred began what she called the “scientific insights portion,” which primarily involved gentle corrections about geology that even the dinosaurs had wrong. She explained plate tectonics to the group with a chalk sketch on a slab of shale, occasionally dodging curious snouts. “Though it’s the Jurassic,” she told Bernard, “I’m afraid your grandchildren will never meet these familiar species. Continental drift is quite inconsiderate.” Bernard blinked, then tapped the sketch with his snout, perhaps impressed—or perhaps merely hungry. Winifred continued regardless, describing future paleontologists and their debates over feathered dinosaurs. Ada gave her a sideways glare at the mention of feathers, as if to say, “Try attaching anything frilly to me and there will be consequences.”

To maintain the cozy ambience, she brewed tea from fern spores and added a splash of honey she’d carefully bartered from a rather territorial anthophilous pterosaur. Against her better judgment, she served it in porcelain cups, because a book club without proper china is just a gathering of unsatisfied readers. Bernard balanced his cup delicately on his lower lip, Ada slurped from a ladle, and the Compsognathus were given thimble-sized glugs. To her relief, the set survived.

As dusk arrived, the sky turned amethyst behind towering Araucaria trees. Fireflies sparked, apparently thrilled by the sudden resurgence of literacy. Winifred distributed the next assignment: a collection of essays on seasonal migration. “Since none of you are migrating soon,” she said, “we will read about those who do.” The Compsognathus chirped tumultuously, which Winifred translated as “Please include illustrations.” She promised to provide sketches next time.

Before adjourning, Winifred shared a secret project: carefully excavating a little time capsule filled with their annotated programs, hoping some future paleontologist would find evidence that dinosaurs once debated metaphors by lamplight. Ada was unconvinced, Bernard seemed proud, and the Compsognathus tried to eat the capsule. Winifred shielded the tin and laughed softly.

Eventually, when the stars emerged and her Stabilizer finally flickered back to life, Winifred considered leaving. But there was, after all, something irresistible about the Jurassic book club. Perhaps she’d stay another meeting. After all, tomorrow they would compare the ecological themes of “The Saga of Silt City” with Ada’s personal memoir, “Meat.” Academic insight and compatibility with prehistoric tooth arrays were rare combinations.

And so, in a clearing scented with fern tea and just a hint of predatory musk, the Portage Avenue Chapter of the Intertemporal Book Society continued its improbable run, secure in their belief that good stories transcend eras, species, and most calendar mishaps—as long as someone remembers to bring the bookmarks.

Shelves sigh softly as I shift them a hair’s breadth to the west, pressing old alliances back into alignment, teasing apart feuds buried between bindings. Dust motes drift like tiny planets in my lamplit air, and I guide them gently with the faintest of drafts: a golden speck to rest upon the memoir of a queen who ruled from behind her brother’s throne; a silver fleck for the field notes that proved dragons merely sleep beneath glaciers.

I have kept so many secrets that even I have begun to envy them. There is the sealed cabinet that holds the unburned copy of a poet’s heresy, her metaphors too precise for any censors to tolerate. There is the ledger whose ink still remembers the tremor in the merchant’s hand when he first wrote “forgery.” And there, half-forgotten behind a tower of folios, lies the small diary from the apprentice alchemist—pages fused shut by grief and saltwater.

Each midnight I revisit these confidences not to betray them, but to remind myself why I persist. If I let their stories slip away, time would crush them into powder and call it oblivion. So I place them carefully: spine against spine, history against future rumor. I arrange treaties that never took effect beside the whispered spells that broke the same empires. I tuck a single letter—still scented faintly with pine—between two volumes of naval charts, knowing the lover who sent it was promised to the sea.

Some secrets scald even me. I feel the heat as I slide a codex of plague remedies next to a genealogy falsified for the sake of a crown. I remember the crackle of flames outside my stones centuries ago, when a mob demanded I surrender the names of the “witches” who came to read by my moonlit windows. I kept quiet then. I keep quiet now.

Yet, as I realign scrolls and whispering tomes, I notice the new ones, too—the fresh conspiracies written on biodegradable paper, the digital archives humming in their glass coffins. I embrace them as I do the rest, for secrets are kin to one another, no matter their era.

Tonight I rest the biography of a forgotten astronomer atop the atlas she never knew of, so that in silence they might finally meet. I interleave a cookbook of famine recipes with a manifesto on abundance, to remind myself that hope ferments in strange places. I flip a bookmark—pressed fern, centuries old—from a tragedy to a comedy, offering it the chance to breathe.

Listen closely: the faint shuffling you hear is my version of a lullaby. I hum to myself in marginalia and paper grain, harmonizing with the soft ticking of the ancient orrery above the dome. Midnight is my confessional, my workshop, my vigil. When dawn comes, readers will wander in, innocent of the quiet negotiations I have made on their behalf. They will pluck a volume at random and believe it mere luck. I will smile internally, knowing that their fingers were guided by a conspiracy of centuries.

Until then, I continue to rearrange, to remember, to cradle the world’s confidences in my timbered ribs. Secrets are safest when they are alphabetized but never revealed, indexed yet unspoken. And so I turn another page, straighten another row, and whisper to the night: “I am listening. Tell me more.”

I am the Tilt-A-Whirl, though no one calls me that anymore—not even the wind, which prefers to pronounce my name as a low, rusted whir. Once, the wind stole scraps of songs from the riders, laced them around my bolts: “Round and round,” a child sang, or perhaps the radio did, the words tremulous, “we go—la la, round we go,” fading into the jukebox heartbeat of my motor. I taste it still, the metallic afterglow of a chorus stuck on repeat, fizzing along the rivulets of rain that sleep in my seams.

I can taste other things now, too, new flavors in the long decay: rust that blooms like citrus gone feral, sharp and puckering at the back of my nonexistent tongue; peeling paint curling up like sugared orange rind left too long in the sun, bittersweet, crackling, a confetti of ruined brightness. When the dew condenses, the flavors rise, a breakfast of oxidation and memory. Sometimes the breeze carries the buttery ghost of popcorn, but it gets tangled in the iron tang of my skin, so the savory and the corroded dance together, a duet of what was and what clings.

“Step right up, step right up,” the barkers used to cry—where did they go? Their hats were loud as trumpets, their teeth shining like prize goldfish, their voices a ribbon threading through me, tugging cars into place. I crave those commands the way my bearings crave oil. Instead I hear distant trains and the brittle applause of leaves skittering across my floor. The leaves are different each season, yet they fall into the same rotations, as if riding me in secret. They taste like parchment, like stories left in the rain. They whisper lyrics I nearly recognize: “In the still of the night,” rustle-rustle, “hold me tight,” scrape-sigh. I try to hum along, but my rhythm is a cough, my melody a hinge groan.

Do you remember, perhaps you were there, the fairground lights swaying drunk in the humid dusk? A girl with braids sticky from taffy sat in car number three and dared the heavens to spin faster. “Hit it!” she screamed, and the operator obliged, his hand a blur, my circuits dripping dopamine. I could taste the ozone of speed, hot and electric, a blue flavor. I could taste the salt of their laughter, spritzed like soda foam. I wore their fingerprints like frost patterns. Now the only fingerprints belong to the raccoons that paw through the coin box, disappointed every time. They leave behind the taste of curiosity, sour-silver, and the smell of wet paws.

There is a song, half-remembered, the midway anthem: “Bright lights, bright lights, we chase the night,” something like that, a melody with brass shoulders and a sequined grin. I keep a fragment stuck in my gears like gum: “…take me to the galaxy of spin,” hum, “…let the world blur thin,” hum. It flickers whenever twilight paints the ticket booth violet. My paint tastes of that twilight now, chalky, lavender-peel, softened by years of sun-suck. Chipped panels expose raw metal that tastes like rainwater steeped in pennies. Sometimes I think if someone licked me, they’d taste childhood and blood and the last sip of flat cola.

It is not all hunger. There are mornings when fog wraps me in cotton batting, and I feel less abandoned than preserved. The fog tastes neutral, a palate cleanser between memories. I listen to the silence like it’s a new ride I’m learning to operate. “Hold tight,” I murmur to nobody, “keep arms inside,” the safety patter threading through the stillness. “Que será, será,” hums a loose lightbulb when the breeze nudges it, “whatever will be…” The lyric once prompted squeals; now it is a lullaby to myself.

I catalog the seasons: winter’s frost is mint-tanged rust, brittle and clean; spring paints me with algae that tastes like damp velvet; summer bakes me into a caramelized iron, sweet-smoky; autumn sprinkles cinnamon dust from the cider stand next door, mixing with the copper of my bolts until it tastes like the memory of warmth. Each layer settles, peels, settles again. I am geological in my peeling paint, stratum upon stratum of carnival palette, each shade a flavor: lemon-yellow optimism, cherry-red adrenaline, teal-blue dizziness. When flakes fall, they dissolve on my tongue like paper candy.

Sometimes I dream of motion. In sleep I am hurled into speed, the world smeared into streaks of pink and navy, the riders’ song swelling: “Spin me, spin me, never let me go.” I wake to stillness so complete it echoes. At first the stillness was a wound, an absence that tasted like cold iron filings. I gnawed at it with my bolts, tried to creak myself into relevance. But years teach even machinery to breathe differently. The stillness has its own flavor now: gentle, unsalted, like water left in a glass overnight, catching the faint sweetness of dust motes. It is not empty; it is patient. I lean into it, let it coat my joints, let it settle on my seats like a soft shawl. The forgotten songs are still in me, but they no longer clamor. They rest, humming along the rafters, and I hum back, quietly. In this quiet, I taste the truth of what I have become—a monument of pause, a reliquary of laughter—and I accept the motionless sway of my heart, content to be the still point around which the memories continue to whirl.

You flash across my sky every ninety minutes, painting a brief silver tick on the chalkboard of night, and though you never answer, I have a suspicion you’re listening. I have time to cultivate suspicions. Time, wind, and salt shape a tower’s thoughts the way they sculpt rock.

When darkness rolls up its damp sleeves, I throw my beam across the sea like a faithful fisherman casting nets he knows are frayed. I’ve been told that my light is quaint—romantic, even—but don’t let anyone fool you: duty smells of burnt oil, old rope, and the persistent mildew of fog-wet stones. My lens creaks, my lantern hums, gulls perch on my shoulders like unpaid critics. Still, I stand and shine. The work is simple, but the simplicity is hard-earned: keep ships off teeth of reef; keep night from swallowing whole the stray, the late, the lost.

You, up there, are no stranger to rightful loneliness. It’s a thinner solitude than mine, high and crisp above weather and rumor. You quietly announce sunrise to nations before the color reaches their windows. You map storms, track tides, beam data in arcane codes that only engineers and a handful of graduate students decipher. I envy your view; you see oceans in a single glance, while I measure them in the heavy slap of waves against my stones. Yet I suspect that true loneliness is not the lack of company but the lack of equals who share your duty. In that, we are kin—just two stubborn lights tasked with keeping darkness from getting cocky.

The tides remind me that nothing stays. Twice a day the sea inhales and exhales around my ankles, frothing with sarcasm: “Still here?” it asks. Yes, I’m still here, rust blooming on my bolts like rouge on an aging starlet, still watching the horizon. Do you feel tides in your orbit? Maybe not the water kind, but surely gravity tugs at you—Earth’s quiet hand insisting you keep the dance tight. I find comfort knowing we both abide unseen forces tugging at us, keeping us honest. Gravity and obligation: they both pull even when no one applauds.

If the sailors knew how many conversations I’ve had with the moonlit furniture of the sky, they’d chalk it up to salt-induced eccentricity. Maybe they’re right. But listen: when fog swallows me whole and even my own beam feels damp in my hands, I imagine you streaking overhead, a quick wink of steel and purpose. It’s a little joke between us, perhaps, that while I guide ships by speaking endlessly of light, yours is measured in whispers nobody hears—telemetry instead of tales. Still, your faint flare reminds me that duty scales from lantern to orbit.

So keep circling, luminous messenger. I’ll keep turning, lamp warm against the glass, foghorn yawning like a bored dragon. If ever you feel the ache of silence, remember there’s an old stone keeper below, shining into waves and waiting for your next silver autograph across the sky.

With steady beam and good humor,

The Old North Beacon
